Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Juan Hernandez had always been a man who cherished his independence, but after what happened in 'Nam, everything changed. It started with the smell of diesel fuel and the acrid taste that lingered on his tongue long after he'd left the battlefield. Even now, 40 years later, the mere whiff of diesel or that same bitter taste would send him reeling - dizzy and disoriented, like he was back in the midst of chaos. As a special education teacher, Juan had always prided himself on being able to connect with his students, but after the war, he found himself increasingly avoiding situations that might stir up strong emotions. He'd steer clear of parent-teacher conferences or staff meetings, opting instead for solo projects that allowed him to maintain a safe distance from others. This self-imposed isolation wasn't just about emotional comfort; it was also about survival - in his mind, if he didn't feel like he was in control, he might as well be back in the trenches. When Juan did venture out into public spaces, he'd always make sure to scope out the nearest exit, mentally mapping escape routes before he felt comfortable enough to focus on anything else. This wasn't just about being prepared; it was an instinct honed from years of living with the constant threat of ambush. Loud noises would still startle him - the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming shut could send his heart racing - and Juan would find himself scanning his surroundings, searching for signs of danger. As time went on, these habits only intensified. Juan became increasingly hypervigilant, always "on" and ready to respond to potential threats that others might not even notice. This perpetual state of high alert made it difficult for him to relax, even in the safety of his own home. And yet, paradoxically, this constant threat monitoring also seemed to trigger more flashbacks - he'd find himself reliving the horrors of war, his mind flooded with images and sounds that he thought he'd long buried. Talking about the event itself was still almost impossible for Juan; even after all these years, the memories remained too raw, too painful. But what really frightened him was the way these memories seemed to be seeping into other areas of his life - how a simple smell or taste could transport him back to that godforsaken place. It was as if the past was slowly closing in on him, and Juan wasn't sure how much longer he could keep it at bay. Lately, Juan's been feeling like he's losing ground - the avoidance behaviors that used to feel like a necessary evil now seem like they're strangling him. His relationships with his students are suffering, and even his own family is starting to notice the changes in him. That's what finally brought Juan to seek help: the realization that if he didn't confront these demons once and for all, he risked losing everything - including himself.
